title: How to tell if a recruiter is legit
summary: How to tell if a recruiter is legit: check the person, their email domain and the company separately. Sixtyfour researches all three and cites every source.
body_markdown:
Check the recruiter, the email address and the company separately, then check that they connect. A real recruiter works at the company they name, writes from that company's own domain and is hiring for a role listed on its careers page. Find the company's website and phone number yourself, never through the message, and stop if anyone asks you to pay, buy equipment or send ID and bank details before a formal hire.


Find the company's website yourself and compare its domain with the one in the email, one character at a time, looking for a dropped or doubled letter, an extra word or a different ending. A free webmail address or a domain registered weeks ago for an established company is a strong warning sign. A recruiter from an agency writes from the agency's domain, so check the agency the same way.


Look for a workplace verification on the profile, shown in its About this member section, and for a Verified Recruiter label on InMails sent through a company's LinkedIn Recruiter licence. A missing badge proves little, because these verifications depend on the company and its subscription, so check whether the person is connected to colleagues at the company and appears on the company's own pages. A verified profile does not prove that an email using the same name came from that person.


No. The FTC says "Honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job", and that honest placement firms do not typically charge candidates a fee. The FBI lists a requirement to buy start-up equipment from the company among the signs of a hiring scam, and says legitimate employers ask for bank details for payroll after hiring.


Find the role on the company's own careers page, confirm it with the company on a phone number from its website, and check that the hiring process looked like a real one. A real offer follows interviews in person or on video, and does not ask you to pay, buy equipment, deposit a cheque or send ID and bank details before you are hired. Pressure to move to a messaging app and decide quickly is a reason to slow down.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes a recruiter's name, email address and claimed employer, researches where the person works today, whether the email domain belongs to the company and whether the company lists the role, and returns each finding with its source and, when you ask for one, a confidence score. Anything it could not establish is reported as open, and you decide what to do.


Stop replying, send nothing, and do not open further links or attachments from them. Report the messages to the platform they came through, to the FTC and to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, and tell the company that was impersonated. If you paid, contact the bank or payment service you used at once and ask it to reverse the transaction if it can.
